Title: Jensen Huang's ouster likely traces back to Nvidia's risky business practices more than his personal life

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/jensen-huangs-ouster-likely-traces-back-to-nvidias-risky-business-practices-more-than-his-personal-life/

Published Time: 2026-11-13T20:07:34+00:00

Markdown Content:
**A WSJ report suggests Jensen Huang was pushed out more over his business practices than over his affairs.**

Nvidia built a risky credit program under Huang, the [Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/tech/jensen-huang-colette-kress-nvidia-ceo-eb289097) reports. The company offered AI cloud providers and data center developers billions of dollars in financial guarantees so they could afford Nvidia chips. Huang's son-in-law Nico Caprez pushed the program and promised partners quick closings. In return, the cloud providers were supposed to give Nvidia a cut of their revenue.

## "A deer in the headlights"

The largest deal involved talks with OpenAI over a $250 billion guarantee for a data center in Ohio. Nvidia shares fell 5% after the deal became public. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who had been CFO, then [cut Nvidia's commitment to OpenAI in half](https://the-decoder.com/investor-pressure-forces-nvidia-to-shrink-its-openai-bet-just-as-anthropics-numbers-defy-bubble-warnings/). The scaled-back deal was signed in August.

According to the WSJ, Kress had already questioned internally how the guarantees were valued and what they would return and had tried to rein in Caprez. In an August meeting, Huang reportedly called her "a deer in the headlights" and dismissed her as a mere "reporting CFO" who didn't help him with strategy or decision-making. Circular AI deals by Nvidia and other cloud and chip companies have drawn criticism since at least last year [for inflating a bubble](https://the-decoder.com/openai-has-now-signed-1-trillion-worth-of-ai-infrastructure-contracts/).

Nvidia's stock valuation also reportedly frustrated Huang. The company's average monthly stock multiple fell from 23 to 16 between May and October, and Nvidia responded with the largest share buyback in its history.

## Huang apparently feared he had made a losing bet

Major cloud providers were planning to adopt alternative chips and reduce their dependence on Nvidia. With Nvidia committed to buying large volumes of wafers and memory, Huang described the threat as an “avalanche” rolling toward the chipmaker.

At the GTC conference in Berlin in October, Huang used a story about a soup vendor in Japan to put pressure on half a dozen cloud CEOs. He said he had stood in a long line and eaten one of the best soups of his life. When he asked for seconds, the vendor said no because too many people were waiting and he was running out of soup. "He's a better businessperson than all of you," Huang told the CEOs, according to the WSJ.

The reasoning behind the story was that the soup vendor didn't sell his whole inventory to one or two customers. He kept prices high and his customer base broad. Huang said the cloud providers weren't following that example and were selling too much compute to a handful of big customers instead of spreading it across many buyers. "You are not establishing the value of my products," Huang said.

Whether Huang left voluntarily because the situation was slipping away from him, which seems unlikely, or whether the board saw an opportunity to use the affairs as leverage, hasn't been reported.

Separately, the spy allegations involving Alice Huang rest on shaky ground, [according to CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/12/politics/alice-huang-us-intel-jensen-huang-nvidia). The intelligence gathered so far doesn't prove she actually worked as a spy for Beijing. Even within the US government, there's disagreement about the strength of the evidence.

A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem
Haskell Foundation
hasufell
November 13, 2026,  5:03am
1
Hi all,
the
technical leadership committee
of the Haskell Foundation has been successfully bootstrapped!
We have spent the last few weeks discussing our vision and strategy and are now fully operational.
We’re going to actively develop initiatives and proposals that we believe need funding and execution. For that we need companies, contractors and volunteers to help. Everyone can participate, whether it’s by dropping ideas informally, writing a concrete proposal themselves or finding entities that could support or fund initiatives.
We tried to keep the
community proposal process
as light as possible. However, we believe that
fairness
and
participation
are vital, especially when funding is involved, so anyone who writes a proposal should be aware that we will open the floor for the community to comment or even deliver counter-proposals. The process may evolve as we make experiences and get feedback.
Below is our vision. Feel free to
get in touch
with us!
The TLC’s shared vision
We believe that Haskell is awesome and that it can provide unique value to everyone, because it sits at an interesting intersection between human craftsmanship and machine automation:
It is good for humans to write by hand: Type safety, powerful abstractions and referential transparency have enabled engineers all over the world in startups and big tech to deliver and maintain complex systems.
It is good for responsible AI workflows: review is a significant bottleneck in modern AI-workflows and Haskell’s strengths heavily favor the reviewer. Additionally, the ability to quickly design eDSLs and express constraints where it matters allows to set up strong guardrails for code generation, without losing flexibility.
There may be better languages for formal verification or for vibecoding, but there’s no better language for “human in the loop”. Haskell is where we maintain control of our work, build institutional knowledge and ship responsibly.
We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone:
Beginners: the onboarding experience must be our benchmark for usability
Experts: enabling advanced workflows and improving productivity
Industry: focussing on stability and scaling
A vision of productivity
Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance!
Iteration speed
Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows.
While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2.
Debugging and profiling
Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries:
live step-through debugging
actually useful stack traces
beautiful performance analysis reports
And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP).
Debugging must be fun again, without littering
Debug.Trace.trace
all over your codebase.
Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools.
Onboarding and DevX
In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole.
installation so quick that you’re wondering whether the installer even worked
documentation so comprehensive and accessible that you never get stuck
tooling so intuitive that you don’t have to constantly ask for support
This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as:
write programs that do one thing and do it well
write programs that work together
write programs that are extensible
Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans.
A vision of a secure and trustworthy ecosystem
Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost.
To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to:
have the fastest incident response time among language ecosystems
have penetration testers go through our infrastructure regularly
make end users aware of vulnerabilities and mitigations
build a robust cryptography library stack
harden our supply chain
We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of
dependent types
and
liquidhaskell
.
A vision of stability
What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes?
While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway.
The questions we need to answer along the way are:
how can users opt out of breaking changes?
how long can we keep support windows open?
how can we make the upgrade experience better?
Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn.
We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem.
A vision of a flourishing open source ecosystem
All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other.
We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world.
We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values.

Title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories

URL Source: https://text.npr.org/nx-s1-6029408

Markdown Content:
By Sequoia Carrillo

Friday, November 13, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST

[_Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly._](https://text.npr.org/newsletter/ed)

* * *

Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.

[An announcement this month](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/) makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.

Many parents do not.

"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."

* * *

Related Story: [NPR](https://text.npr.org/nx-s1-6022278)

* * *

When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group [Schools Beyond Screens](https://www.schoolsbeyondscreens.com/), first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding [limits on technology in the classroom](https://text.npr.org/2026/05/01/nx-s1-5791657/states-schools-restricting-screen-time).

But even as districts including [Los Angeles Unified](https://text.npr.org/2026/08/11/nx-s1-5913745/screen-limits-begin-la-schools), [Seattle Public Schools](https://www.kuow.org/education/2026-11-05/seattle-public-schools-tightens-student-access-to-youtube-minecraft-and-ai) and [New York City Public Schools](https://text.npr.org/2026/09/02/nx-s1-5954196/ai-is-everywhere-nyc-schools-want-to-keep-it-away-from-young-kids) recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.

In [a post on X](https://x.com/NYCMayor/status/2117692668213940677), New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts [wrote to Google's CEO](https://www.markey.senate.gov/news/press-releases/markey-demands-google-allow-schools-to-disable-ai-services-without-blocking-search-access) demanding the company reverse its policy.

### **A baffling move**

Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.

She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google [fended off](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/google-wins-dismissal-chegg-penske-media-lawsuits-over-ai-overviews-2026-10-01/) in D.C.

Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.

"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."

When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its [original announcement](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/), where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.

NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.

### The "AI or nothing" approach

In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "[unacceptable risk](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/articles/google-ai-overview-cant-turn-it-off)" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.

The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina [sued](https://edtech.law/cases/emma-v-google/) the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.

Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.

* * *

Related Story: [NPR](https://text.npr.org/nx-s1-5938800)

* * *

"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.

Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.

He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.

"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."

The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.

_Google is a financial supporter of NPR._

Title: Anthropic Upgrades Claude Code Projects to Run Parallel AI Workers Hands-Free

URL Source: https://alphasignal.ai/news/anthropic-upgrades-claude-code-projects-to-run-parallel-ai-workers-hands-free

Published Time: 2026-11-13T22:51:01.000Z

Markdown Content:
Anthropic has updated [Claude Code Projects](https://claude.com/form/projects?utm_source=alphasignal) with proactive coordinator messages, read-only thread sharing, reminders, branching commands, and improved artifact navigation. The changes reduce the monitoring required when several cloud sessions work in parallel.

Each project is a long-running conversation with a coordinator that assigns work to threads. Every thread runs as an independent Claude Code cloud session with its own repository copy and Git branch. The coordinator directs the project from thread reports, while overlapping code changes surface as standard Git merge conflicts when branches are combined.

## The coordinator reports without prompting

The coordinator now answers questions directly in project chat and posts status updates as threads progress. Previously, developers had to monitor the thread list to find sessions waiting for input. The updated behavior brings pending decisions, completed tasks, and blocked work into the main conversation.

## Read-only links stop at local access

Individual threads can now be shared through read-only links with anyone signed in to Claude. A developer can open the thread menu, select **Share**, and send the generated URL without exposing the rest of the project.

Threads that accessed a local computer remain unshareable. The restriction prevents shared transcripts from exposing local file contents, shell output, or other machine data gathered during the session.

## Park a thread or branch the work

| Control | Behavior | Best use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Reminders** | Hide a thread until a specified time, then return it to the thread list and notify the coordinator. | Work that depends on a later review, deployment, or external response. |
| `/btw` | Open a separate thread for a tangent while preserving the current thread’s goal and context. | Investigating a related issue without diverting active work. |
| `/fork` | Create a new thread from the current thread’s state. | Testing an alternative implementation or debugging path. |

The two slash commands were already available in regular Claude Code sessions. Their addition to Projects brings the same branching workflow to coordinated, multi-thread work.

## Artifacts surface sooner

The threads panel now places recently opened, updated, and pinned threads in a row at the top. Each thread can also display thumbnails for generated documents, diagrams, and other artifacts, with the previews controlled through view settings.

The redesign simplifies project settings and local-folder access as well. Anthropic has released the changes on the web, desktop clients, and the latest mobile app.

## Parallelism draws from the same allowance

Anthropic introduced the public beta on September 17 for Pro and Max subscribers who joined the waitlist. Team and Enterprise plans remain unsupported. Eligible subscribers who lack access can still [join the waitlist](https://claude.com/form/projects?utm_source=alphasignal).

Projects carry no separate fee, but every worker consumes the subscriber’s existing Claude Code allowance. Anthropic limits accounts to 200 new threads per day across all projects. A thread that reaches a usage limit pauses and resumes automatically when capacity becomes available.

Project usage appears separately in the usage controls, and developers can choose the model and effort level for the coordinator and worker threads. New projects default to Opus for both roles, with low effort for the coordinator and high effort for workers. Several high-effort sessions running at once can exhaust plan limits faster than a single Claude Code session.

## Where many threads pay off

Projects fit engineering work that can be divided into independent tasks and reconciled through branches and pull requests. Anthropic’s examples include:

*   **Performance work:** Assign separate threads to profile endpoints, test optimizations, and open pull requests. A target such as p75 checkout latency refers to the response time at or below which 75% of requests finish.
*   **Cross-repository migrations:** Connect API, web, and mobile repositories, then create one thread per codebase and report the required merge order.
*   **Batch changes:** Distribute refactors, dependency upgrades, test repairs, or bug-triage items across parallel sessions.

Tasks with strict dependencies still require developers to sequence pull requests and resolve conflicts. Projects also remain cloud-only and limited to Claude Code, while parallel workers draw from the same plan limits. Small changes that fit one branch and one context window generally consume fewer resources in a regular Claude Code session.

articles.content:
Title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models

URL Source: https://haddyalchaer.com/jepa

Published Time: 2026-11-11

Markdown Content:
World models · JEPA · Planning

By Haddy Alchaer · November 2026

Solving long-horizon tasks without any extra training

0/16 on target · step  26

Vanilla LeWM can be augmented to solve long-horizon physics tasks on out-of-distribution goals. This method uses transformations on a memory graph to generate on-the-fly subgoals without any additional training. Shown here are some of the hardest tasks it solved.

There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [[1]](https://haddyalchaer.com/jepa#ref-1)

The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions.

The three parts of a JEPA world model.

This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [[2]](https://haddyalchaer.com/jepa#ref-2), a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [[3]](https://haddyalchaer.com/jepa#ref-3), a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it.

A goal image from Push-T

The planner is given an image like this one and has to make the scene match it. The gray T is the block, the blue disc is the robot's pusher, and the green T is the goal position painted on the table. One detail in this image turned out to affect the success rate more than replacing the predictor with simulated physics.

The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are _already_ as good as perfect physics for planning.

Success on 250 long-horizon tasks

78%

Vanilla LeWM

learned predictor

77%

LeWM real physics

the simulator itself

That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went.

Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did.

## 1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart

Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [[2]](https://haddyalchaer.com/jepa#ref-2) When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%.

So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks.

250 long-horizon tasks, goal 75 steps away

LeWM, all 75 steps at once as published

22%

Exact physics, all 75 steps at once the simulator itself

42%**+20**

LeWM given a new subgoal every 25 steps same model, shorter hops

80%**+58**

0 25 50 75 100%

Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together.

LeWM's planning horizon is about 25 steps

Plan all 75 steps at once ... one search, far goal 22%

A subgoal every 25 steps ... three short searches 80%

Chaining 25-step searches through subgoals keeps every search inside the range where LeWM is accurate.

This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics.

Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together.

The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence.

## 2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump

LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals.

This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach.

The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the _same score_ received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right?

Planning through a memory of demonstrations

start goal

Each thin path is one demonstration. With free jumps, the shortest route hops between demonstrations into a path the block can't physically follow. With a cost per jump, it stays on them.

## The standard Push-T test is easier than it looks

The caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration.

demonstrations, all ending in about the same place goals in the standard test goals from other demonstrations

The standard test picks its goals along these streams. The harder test asks for goals like the orange ones, which no single demonstration leads to.

The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing _nothing but the planner's random seed_ flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure.

That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap.

## 3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories

A memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%.

Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%).

Filling a gap in memory with transformed demonstrations

a demonstration segment from elsewhere the same segment, shifted, rotated or mirrored

Block reached its target, 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away)

93%full memory

32%states near the goal deleted

85%gap filled with rotated and mirrored copies

On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%.

Harder test, by where the goal lies

about 83 tasks per row

Goal lies with the flow of the demonstrations

39%54%

## 4. The cost was “wrong”

I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image.

21 px from target off target

The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too.

To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s.

Block held on target, same 50 tasks

exact-physics planner

Block and pusher 9 / 50

Block only 39 / 50

success with either cost**30**succeed only without the pusher**0**succeed only with the pusher included

Thirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from _how the goal was created_.

Title: Introducing Claude Meetings

URL Source: https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-meetings

Published Time: 2026-11-12

Markdown Content:
Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta.

Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission.

Claude also works with you live to build docs, [whiteboards (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data), or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to.

Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon.

## What it looks like

Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking.

When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc.

Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in [claude.ai (opens in new tab)](http://claude.ai/redirect/claudedotcom.v1.87ecab94-ed14-421b-af66-f93f044b276f).

Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai.

We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, Otter, and Plaud, so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses.

## Security and privacy

Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in [claude.ai (opens in new tab)](http://claude.ai/redirect/claudedotcom.v1.87ecab94-ed14-421b-af66-f93f044b276f) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page.

By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript.

Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call.

When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio.

Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed.

## Getting started

Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, [whiteboards, (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027.

Setup steps are in the [Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/18325154).

articles.content:
Title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

URL Source: https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/13/kurt-godel-notebooks-ai-helps-unlock-hidden-discoveries-man-who-transformed-maths

Published Time: 2026-11-13T16:38:27.000Z

Markdown Content:
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two [incompleteness theorems](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2022/jan/10/can-you-solve-it-godels-incompleteness-theorem), published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.

After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.

The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive

“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled [Austria](https://www.theguardian.com/world/austria) under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.

“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.

“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”

after newsletter promotion

A microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced Study

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.

Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.

The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”

Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”

In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: _falsch!_ [incorrect] or _schlecht!_ [bad].”

Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”

Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”

Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out 36% of Russia’s total oil refining capacity in less than two weeks, hitting at least nine major refineries between Oct. 30 and Nov. 11, defense manufacturer Fire Point [reported](https://t.me/firepointofficial/502) on Nov. 12.

articles.content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”
The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says
Ian Burkhart
, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).
Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”
Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.
He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm,
allowing him to control it
.
The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was
a scientific breakthrough
.
Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”
In 2022, Burkhart cofounded
BCI Pioneers Coalition
—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.
The guidelines,
published on Tuesday
, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”
As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.
The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.
Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’
brain data
. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.
The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.
“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”
The guidelines also address what comes
after
a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When
we last spoke a few years ago
, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about
brain surgery
here.)
Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.
Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later,
the device was removed against her will
—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.
Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.
Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still
very low
. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an
upcoming neuroscience conference
.
“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”
